articles.title: Introducing Wiz ADR: Strengthening Cloud and AI Detection and Response with Application Context
articles.context: AI-assisted attacks have dramatically compressed the time from vulnerability disclosure to active exploitation–meaning attackers routinely reach execution faster than...
articles.full_text:
The security tools SecOps teams rely on have gotten exceptionally good at detecting infrastructure-level events: subprocess spawns, outbound network connections, and system calls. However, what has historically been missing is visibility into the application layer sitting directly above those events: which specific function executed the call, how code execution reached that point, and whether the observed runtime behavior represents expected application logic or an active exploit in progress.

This visibility gap is becoming increasingly critical to address. AI-assisted attacks have dramatically compressed the time from vulnerability disclosure to active exploitation–meaning attackers routinely reach execution faster than engineering teams can patch. At the same time, modern threats like compromised dependencies and prompt-injected AI agents execute entirely inside legitimate application processes without a CVE at all. When every minute counts, deep application context lets SecOps teams immediately separate real attacks from benign app behavior, pinpoint how execution happened, and respond without delay.

Today, we are excited to announce Wiz ADR (Application Detection and Response). Built directly into the Wiz Runtime Sensor, Wiz ADR brings application-layer visibility into threat detection–pairing application call stacks with OS and process telemetry, with no extra agents or code changes required. Rather than only alerting on suspicious events at the system layer, Wiz ADR reveals the exact functions that triggered them–helping SecOps cut false positives by seeing the application’s true intent, and simplifying the handoff to engineering by pinpointing the exact line of code to fix.

Wiz ADR: Turning Runtime Alerts into Clear Intent and Fast Fixes

Whenever a runtime detection fires across your workloads, the Wiz Runtime Sensor doesn’t stop at the OS process–it reaches into the application layer to capture what your code was doing at the exact moment the event occurred.

Wiz ADR reconstructs the application call stack both inside the process that triggered the alert and across parent-to-child spawns–so even when a web service launches a child shell command, analysts see the exact application function that kicked it off. Along the way, it flags meaningful execution patterns with application context tags (such as Request Handler, Dynamic Code Execution, or Unsafe Deserialization), translating raw function calls into plain-English security signals so SecOps can spot the root cause immediately, even without knowing the underlying codebase. When those context tags appear on a runtime event, the Sensor also uses them directly to trigger high-fidelity application detections and elevate the severity of existing alerts.

Paired with the broader Wiz Platform, that application context turns ambiguous alerts into confirmed verdicts and code-level fixes across two everyday scenarios.

Confirming a Real Exploit with Wiz Blue Agent

Consider a containerized Python FastAPI service that unexpectedly spawns /usr/bin/id as root. On its own, /user/bin/id is too common across Linux workloads for standard OS-level rules to alert on without flooding the SOC–meaning early post-exploitation reconnaissance routinely slips by unnoticed.

With Wiz ADR, the Sensor sees where execution started. It reconstructs the call stack across the process spawn–tracing /user/bin/id back to the import_spellbook HTTP endpoint and into PyYAML’s UnsafeConstructor, attaches context tags like Request Handler, Python Request Handler Descendant, and Unsafe Deserialization, and fires a High-severity alert immediately.

Bringing that stack-trace analysis together with process ancestry and cloud risk gives the Wiz Blue Agent the context to classify the alert as Malicious with high confidence, connecting the application context to root execution inside a privileged production container and pointing teams directly to the import_spellbook endpoint. From there, Wiz Workflows can notify the right teams with full context and trigger response actions to contain the threat immediately.

Eliminating False Positives and Tracing Threats Straight to Code

Now consider the flip side: internal services whose legitimate code triggers scary OS alerts. When repohygiene–a containerized Go service on CI runners–runs find /data -name .git-credentials -type f during post-build audits, OS-level rules flag it as potential credential harvesting.

Pairing Wiz ADR with Wiz Code unlocks Threat to Code correlation, tracing the Go call stack (Scanner.findGitCredentials) straight back to the exact repository, file (scanner.go, line 55) and code owner in GitHub, surfacing the developer’s own code and comments right inside the alert inside of handing engineering a bare container ID and PID.

And with Blue Agent, no human has to triage it manually. Wiz Blue Agent synthesizes the stack trace, clean process ancestry (systemd -> containerd -> runc -> repohygine -> find), and sensor forensics to confirm the activity matches intended application logic, automatically classifying the alert as Not Malicious and deprioritizing it before it burns SecOps hours.

Start Defending Your Environment with Application Context

Wiz ADR is available now through the Wiz Runtime Sensor–giving SecOps and Engineering teams deep application context on runtime detections with no code changes or extra agents required.

Existing Wiz customers can learn more about Wiz ADR in our documentation, and if you are not a customer and want to see it in action please request a demo.

articles.title: A Feast for AI: What Wiz Agents are Thankful For
articles.context: In cloud security, that’s your offensive security team - thinking like real adversaries to uncover exploitable gaps before an attacker does
articles.full_text:
Anyone who has ever survived a family Thanksgiving knows dinner doesn’t just happen. It takes the whole household working in sync to get everyone fed without setting the kitchen on fire, much like how Wiz’s team of AI agents work alongside security, Security Operations, and engineering teams to keep cloud environments running smoothly and securely.

This year each of the agents is taking on a role that suits them at Thanksgiving.

Red Agent is the taste-tester & kitchen inspector: Inspecting every dish against the recipe, probing the turkey for any raw spots, and flagging potential dinner-ruining mistakes before anyone takes a bite.

Green Agent is the head chef & fixer: Tracking down who was responsible for the turkey, figuring out why it’s so dry, and handing out the exact fix - whether that’s adding more butter to save dinner or updating the recipe so this doesn’t happen again.

Blue Agent is the watchful relative: Investigating every smoke alarm in minutes, separating harmless burnt rolls from a real kitchen fire so everyone isn’t sprinting back before they’ve had pie.

This very much lines up with their day jobs. Protecting a cloud environment isn’t a solo act. It takes offensive validation (Red Agent), AI-driven remediation (Green Agent), and autonomous threat investigation (Blue Agent) operating from the same shared context.

As we prepare for the holidays, here is what each of the agents is most thankful for this season.

The Red Agent: Thankful for Real-World Risks Validated Before Attackers Find Them

Every Thanksgiving needs that sharp-eyed family member who makes sure the recipe was actually followed. They taste the stuffing, check the turkey's temperature, and catch the mistakes before anyone else takes a bite. In cloud security, that’s your offensive security team - thinking like real adversaries to uncover exploitable gaps before an attacker does.

Instead of relying on static signature scanners or waiting once a year for a manual pentest, the Red Agent is thankful for continuous, autonomous offensive testing from the outside in. Red Agent uses AI reasoning to understand how an application is built and its business logic so it can uncover complex logic flaws such as authorization bypasses. It continuously pentests your applications at machine-speed enabling you to stay ahead of AI threats.

Red Agent enables your team to find and remove complex logic-driven vulnerabilities before attackers get to them. Better yet, it works together with the Green Agent to give you the exact guidance on how to fix the issues it finds so teams focus their holiday energy on risks in the kitchen that actually matter.

Kitchen Inspector’s tip:A finding is only useful if you can trust it and know where it fits. Red Agent includes full reproduction commands with every finding, so your team can rerun the test and see the issue for themselves. Just as important, Red Agent findings are mapped onto the Wiz Security Graph and generate Wiz Issues. That lets you trace each one back to its blast radius and prioritize it in the context of your cloud environment. A weakness on an isolated test box and one sitting next to sensitive data are very different problems, and now you can tell them apart. That way, you fix the dish that would spoil the whole meal first.

The Green Agent: Thankful for Clear Context and a Recipe for Remediation

Thanksgiving dinner is no easy feat and comes with its fair share of kitchen mishaps. But it’s even harder when no one knows who’s responsible for dinner or how to salvage it before guests arrive. Security and development teams face a similar challenge when it comes to remediation. Alerts bounce between Jira queues with no clear owner, let alone the guidance needed on how to fix them. That meant remediation stretched out for weeks, all the while security teams tried to race toward the Zero Critical Club.

This season, the Green Agent is thankful for the clear context needed to find the right fix. Stepping in like a head chef with a master prep schedule, Green Agent investigates each Issue to determine the owner best positioned to fix it and the best and safest ways to go about fixing it.

All of that comes together in a remediation plan, Green Agent's step-by-step recipe for resolving an Issue. It determines the various ways to eliminate the risks identified in each Issue, whether that’s giving security teams the option to contain or mitigate the risk until a permanent fix is ready or helping developers with the guidance to fix at the root cause in code or harden systems to prevent future risk. Instead of a cold handoff, owners get clear, tailored steps they can act on right away, so fewer dishes get sent back and the team reaches the Zero Critical Club with time to spare.

Chef's Tip: Don't toss the turkey to save the oven

The fastest fix isn't always the right one when you consider the potential business impact. That’s why Green Agent develops multiple remediation plans and uses context from the full environment to weigh the trade-offs of each. For example, examining a front end that’s intentionally public or a workload that’s part of a Project defined as high business impact. It rules out plans that could disrupt critical workloads, giving teams options to reduce risk without taking production down with it. That way, dinner still makes it to the table

The Blue Agent: Thankful for Uninterrupted Quality Time

Finally, there is the watchful relative, checking each smoke alarm the minute it goes off to ensure evacuation is necessary. For Security Operations teams, the ultimate gift isn’t another dashboard; it’s an undisturbed long weekend spent with family and friends.

This year, the Blue Agent is thankful for the context already available on the table, allowing for trusted, complete threat investigations

Threats don’t follow the holiday calendar. Blue investigates threats fired in the environment to understand which ones are truly malicious, running comprehensive investigations powered by the context of the Wiz Security Graph. So, SOC analysts know that the fire alarm they are pulled to investigate is a true positive, instead of leaving family and friends to deal with a drill in the middle of the meal.

Watchful Relative’s Tip: Check the recipe

Most threat investigation tools stop at process or OS-level alerts, leaving analysts guessing what the application was actually trying to do. Blue Agent goes straight to the execution layer by pulling Application Detection and Response (ADR) stack traces during Sensor-based Threat investigations. Seeing the exact application functions in the call stack helps Blue Agent uncover details infrastructure telemetry alone would miss, such as whether an anomaly is harmless app logic or an active exploit like RCE, LFI, or SSRF. This gives SOC teams code-level confirmation before anyone leaves the table.

The Secret Ingredient: A Shared Table

The best Thanksgiving dinners come together when everyone knows their role and cooks from the same recipe. The same is true in the cloud. Red Agent validates exploitable risks, Green Agent turns them into tailored plans to fix them, and Blue Agent investigates live threats. All three work from the same context across the environment, so developers, security engineers, and SecOps can spend more time at the table.

articles.title: Inside Agentic Offensive Frameworks: Intent IDs
articles.context: If a single attacker hits your environment with i14200 at 10:00 and i15100 an hour later, while your logs show only a handful of probes in between, those missing sequence...
articles.full_text:
“Black October” was rife with iNNNN indicators.

Barracuda: i19ghci.yml in a GitHub workflow.

Bitrise: i3694canary as an account name.

Chainstack: artex-i37257 in the attacker's artifacts.

Ardor: i63c2d.py as the persistence poller.

These IDs are Agentic Offensive Framework Intent IDs. We mentioned these IDs in our Agentic Attacks: In The Wild’s ARTEX-Harvester case, and GTIG highlighted them in ARTEX and Friends: Enter Agentic Offensive Frameworks.

We want to dissect them as a new form of harness leak that flows from agentic offensive frameworks into defender logs.

What are Intent IDs?

Intent IDs are incrementing counters in common agentic offensive frameworks. They are an internal implementation detail: the harness breaks an attack into discrete sub-goals called "intents" and assigns each one a numeric ID.

When a harness places that ID in its prompts and workspace paths, it bleeds into the attack: when the model creates a file, registers an account, pushes a GitHub workflow, or sets a User-Agent string on a target, it borrows the identifier sitting right in front of it.

There has been a proliferation of agentic offensive frameworks. We reviewed over a hundred open-source offensive harness repositories, and two families stand out for handing the LLM a numeric Intent ID that leaks into target-side artifacts:

The ARTEX family: ARTEX itself, plus public forks like Pojun (tracking current ARTEX as of v0.4.99) and AntiFox (forked from ARTEX v0.1.1).

The Cairn family: Cairn itself and descendants like sapper-v2 (a reimplementation of Cairn's design).

ARTEX

ARTEX stores intents, facts, findings, hints, and digests in one PostgreSQL table, exploration_nodes, backed by a single BIGSERIAL sequence. Each installation runs its own counter and never resets it by default.

That design produces three traits defenders see in logs:

Numbers climb across runs and targets. A fresh campaign driven from a new ARTEX installation might start in the double digits (i49 through i63 in Ardor's disclosure). A long-running, busy installation climbs into the tens or hundreds of thousands (i37257 at Chainstack).

Intent IDs are rarely seen consecutively increasing. Because facts, findings, hints, and digests draw from the same sequence as intents, consecutive intent numbers are rare.

Facts stay local; intents leak. Workers see fact IDs as bare integers in their planner snapshots. We checked 539 worker transcripts (~10,900 shell commands) from an exposed ARTEX instance. Fact IDs appeared only in local scripts and notes (e.g fact #461).

In agent/worker.go, ARTEX wires the intent ID into three places the model reads on every turn: its working directory (tasks/<task>/i<N>), its session name (exp<N>-worker-i<N>), and the "意图 id" ("intent id") field in its prompt. Pojun keeps this exact layout. AntiFox goes further: its prompt orders the agent to save its outputs under an i<id>/ subdirectory.

Cairn

Cairn separates its counters by object type and leaves a distinct fingerprint.

In services.py, Cairn formats Intent IDs as zero-padded three-digit strings (i%03d) and gives each object type its own series:

Intents: i001, i002, i003...

Facts: f001, f002, f003...

Hints: h001, h002, h003...

Projects: proj_001, proj_002...

Unlike ARTEX, Cairn resets its counters for every new project. Numbers stay small and run without gaps. On one exposed Cairn host we examined, a single project held every intent from i001 through i292.

Cairn passes {intent_id} into its explore prompt as "Current Intent", and the worker reuses it in callbacks, DTD files, webshells, and test accounts.

sapper-v2 reimplements the same i%03d/f%03d/h%03d per-project scheme.

Pacing ARTEX Intent IDs

Because an ARTEX installation's sequence increments across runs and targets without resetting by default, plotting Intent IDs against timestamps can offer analysts a pacing signal.

Linking Across IPs and Incidents

Agentic campaigns often rotate through residential proxy pools, using a new exit IP on nearly every request. Proxy rotation breaks IP-based clustering. Intent IDs cut across that noise: if activity from rotating IPs, or across separate victims, produces Intent IDs climbing at a steady rate over time, those sightings point to one ARTEX installation.

While tracking ARTEX-Harvester, we used rising Intent IDs alongside a distinctive boto3 build and proxy pool overlap to connect activity across more than a dozen organizations.

Intent IDs also survive a move between clouds. In one intrusion the attacker used stolen IAM users in AWS and a service principal in Azure. We found 36 Intent IDs on the AWS side, in SSM command comments and resource names, and 34 on the Azure side, in resource names, tags, and a role assignment description. All of them came from one climbing sequence, linking both to the same run even though the identities have nothing in common.

Deconflicting Installations

The same sequence behavior works in reverse. Because exploration_nodes.id is a single BIGSERIAL counter per database, one ARTEX installation will not assign the same Intent ID to two different intents.

This property gives analysts a rough way to separate instances:

Duplicate IDs across unrelated targets point to separate installations. Two campaigns hitting i13211 against different victims are running on different ARTEX databases, not the same one. (A single worker will reuse its own ID across multiple requests and artifacts while working a single intent, so duplicates within one engagement are expected.)

Out-of-order jumps signal a split. If a cluster of activity shows i37257 on Monday and i4100 on Tuesday, those requests are not coming from one continuous database sequence.

This deconfliction separates installations, not necessarily operators. One operator can run several ARTEX instances in parallel.

Gauging Scope from a Single Victim's Logs

Even without cross-victim visibility, the size of the gaps between Intent IDs could indicate whether your are a dedicated target or one of many.

If a single attacker hits your environment with i14200 at 10:00 and i15100 an hour later, while your logs show only a handful of probes in between, those missing sequence numbers went somewhere. Some of that gap comes from facts, findings, hints, and digests recorded against your own assets. When a jump dwarfs the activity in your logs, the same ARTEX installation is likely burning through tasks against other targets in parallel: an opportunistic, multi-target run rather than an operator focused solely on you.

These signals are lossy. Intent ID pacing is a corroborating signal, not standalone attribution:

The rate of climb is uneven. Facts, findings, hints, and digests share the sequence, and work against other targets advances the counter between sightings at one victim.

Unrelated installations collide in the same numeric ranges. Fresh deployments all pass through the low hundreds and thousands, so two unrelated operators can produce numbers that look sequential by coincidence.

Operators reset or parallelize. Rebuilding the container, wiping the database, or splitting targets across multiple ARTEX instances breaks the sequence.

Cairn resets per project. Because Cairn restarts at i001 for every new project, cross-incident pacing applies only to the ARTEX family.

Intent IDs in the Wild

Across public disclosures, exposed harness directories, and our telemetry, we cataloged hundreds of distinct Intent IDs. A few extremes show how the two designs behave at scale:

Highest Intent ID: i808807. Observed in ARTEX activity in November 2026, alongside pentest-i804759 and i806173 from the same series. An installation only reaches the 800,000s after churning through intents, facts, and findings across targets without a reset.

Lowest Intent ID: i001. The bootstrap intent of a Cairn project recovered from an exposed Cairn host. Cairn's dispatcher creates i001 automatically as a synthetic root edge connecting origin to the project's initial seed fact (f001), before worker intents begin at i002.

Longest consecutive runs:

Cairn: i001 through i292. Every intent present in a complete project graph recovered from an exposed Cairn open directory.

ARTEX: i8920 through i8923 (four in a row). Seen in artex-verify-i89xx User-Agent strings. ARTEX installations rarely string more than a few consecutive Intent IDs together because facts, findings, hints, and digests pull from the same sequence between intents.

Hunting for Harness Leaks

Intent IDs are noisy on their own, so pair i<N> with an anchor before alerting. Good anchors include prefixes like artex-, pentest-, probe, or canary in account names, User-Agents, CI workflows, and cloud resources, or leaked run-directory paths such as tasks/<task>/i<N> in command-line telemetry. Hits are useful tool markers and pacing clues, but not operator fingerprints.

Where do these leak in logs? Anywhere that the API expects user-provided context, naming, or commentary. We have already observed these IDs in:

AWS:

role session names

SSM command comments

bucket, role, user, and policy names

tags and descriptions

RDS export task IDs

KMS key descriptions and aliases

security-group names and rule descriptions

Azure and Entra:

run-command names

VM computer names

app registration names

Note: for denied calls, the names survive in error messages.

articles.title: “Do Good Security” and Other Lessons from Wiz’s FedRAMP VDR & VER Event
articles.context: Wiz recently hosted an event focused around FedRAMP’s new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) requirements
articles.full_text:
Wiz recently hosted an event focused around FedRAMP’s new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) requirements. This event, entitled “The Final Countdown: Supporting FedRAMP VDR & VER Requirements,” brought together industry leaders responsible for maintaining FedRAMP Cloud Service Offerings. With the initial implementation deadline for VDR & VER approaching on December 7th, the event provided a forum to clarify the government's expectations and help cloud service providers navigate the transition from outdated compliance models to modern, continuous security practices.

The centerpiece of the event was an in-depth policy panel featuring subject matter experts from the U.S. Government and leadership from the Cloud Service Providers Advisory Board (CSPAB) alongside Wiz's Head of Government Affairs.

During the discussion, it was emphasized that the core goal of the new policies—often collectively referred to as "VaDER"—is to empower organizations to proactively secure their systems, rather than checking legacy compliance boxes. The panel addressed industry anxieties surrounding compliance timelines, agency reception, and interpretation of the new rules. Following the panel, the event also featured a brief overview and demonstration of the minimal viable product (MVP) capabilities Wiz has introduced to directly support these new VDR requirements, culminating in a Q&A session with industry experts around their operational experiences and lessons learned.

4 Key Takeaways from the Event

Prioritize Real Security Over Compliance: The core philosophy behind the VDR and VER policies is to simply "do good security". Rather than relying on outdated vulnerability scanning, FedRAMP’s VDR & VER requirements focus effective vulnerability detection and response around true risk to agency and customer data.

Embrace the Flexibility: FedRAMP is intentionally avoiding rigid, opinionated guidance on specific tools or methods. This empowers Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) to implement security measures that best fit their unique technical environments, risks, and modern engineering standards.

Pragmatic Deadline Expectations: Panelists discussed details around the upcoming timelines, and discussed how FedRAMP certifications will not be abruptly pulled immediately following the December 7th deadline, provided companies are making a sincere effort to adapt. CSPs will be asked to submit a progress report in December and can utilize corrective action plans for items that require the extended March grace period.

Lead the Way with Agencies: Agency customers may not fully know what to expect from the new reporting formats. CSPs have a unique opportunity to proactively work with their agencies by providing clean, human-readable monthly activity reports that demonstrate the effectiveness of their modern security programs.

Missed the event? Recordings are available

Interested in seeing recordings from the event? Head over to our event summary page to watch the on-demand recordings, hear from government and industry leaders, and see the new Wiz capabilities designed to help your organization accelerate its VDR & VER readiness.

Disclaimer: This content is provided for informational purposes only, does not constitute legal or regulatory advice or imply endorsement by the U.S. Government, FedRAMP, or any third-party organization, and actual compliance outcomes vary by customer environment under a shared responsibility model. Recordings are available for event registrants and other technical practitioners responsible for FedRAMP CSOs who may have missed the registration deadline.

Today, we’re excited to announce Wiz’s integration with OpenAI’s Daybreak Defense Factory through the new Wiz plugin for Codex(login required).

Daybreak Defense Factory uses autonomous agents to discover, validate, and remediate vulnerabilities, helping teams move from raw findings to actionable code fixes. But code doesn't live in a vacuum - effective remediation requires cloud context: Is this workload exposed to the internet? Can it reach sensitive data? Is it tied to high privileges?

Wiz brings that real-world cloud intelligence from the Wiz Security Graph directly into Codex. Together, Wiz and OpenAI are putting AI to work for defenders—enabling teams to trace complex cloud risks back to their code origins and draft targeted pull requests, while keeping security and development teams firmly in control.

From Cloud Risk to Code Fixes with Wiz and Codex

Wiz brings context about cloud exposure, identities, permissions, and sensitive data. Codex uses that context to investigate the underlying code and develop proposed fixes. Together, they help teams understand both why a finding matters and how to address it. An isolated vulnerability or misconfiguration rarely tells the full story. Effective fixes require understanding what's exposed, how risks connect, what an attacker could reach, and where the underlying issue originated.

With the Wiz plugin for Codex, Wiz brings security findings and contextual intelligence from the Wiz Security Graph directly into Codex. Developers ask in plain language, such as "fix the Wiz findings that matter in this repo," and Codex pulls the repository's findings, what it deploys to the cloud, and the context behind each risk through the Wiz MCP server.

This helps teams:

Trace risk to its source: Connect vulnerabilities and misconfigurations to the code, Dockerfile instructions, or infrastructure-as-code definitions where they originated.

Understand the full attack path: Correlate findings with internet exposure, cloud identities, effective permissions, and sensitive data to identify the risks that matter most.

Accelerate remediation: Equip Codex with the context to reproduce vulnerabilities, generate targeted fixes, and prepare pull requests for developer review.

Hand findings to Codex Security: Send a repository's Wiz findings, with cloud context and code owners attached, to Codex Security for validation and triage.

Together, Wiz and OpenAI help organizations move from fragmented alerts and manual investigation toward faster, context-driven remediation, with security and development teams maintaining oversight.

Collective Defense in Action: Patch the Planet

Our work with Daybreak Defense Factory builds on a broader collaboration with OpenAI through the Daybreak Defense Network and coordinated initiatives under Patch the Planet. These efforts share a single objective: giving defenders the collective intelligence, context, and AI capabilities needed to outpace modern threats.

The recent response to critical PHP vulnerabilities (dubbed PHP2Shell) shows what this model delivers in practice:

Collaborative discovery: Wiz independently discovered and responsibly reported vulnerabilities, while cybersecurity consultancy Calif identified a critical flaw using OpenAI models through Patch the Planet.

Maintainer-led remediation: PHP maintainers led the release of upstream fixes, supported by OpenAI, Wiz, and partners contributing patch verification and coordination ahead of public disclosure.

Community-wide protection: This work produced upstream patches, provider mitigations, and immediate customer protection—including vulnerability detection, active exploitation monitoring, and threat-hunting guidance from Wiz.

Daybreak Defense Factory extends this collaborative approach from major vulnerability responses into everyday security operations: helping teams turn shared intelligence into reviewed fixes.

Advancing AI Security Together

Wiz and OpenAI share a fundamental commitment to putting AI on the side of defenders. As a proud partner in OpenAI’s Daybreak Defense Network, Wiz is deepening our strategic collaboration to ensure modern security teams have the collective intelligence and tooling needed to stay ahead of emerging threats.

By embedding the Wiz Security Graph into Daybreak Defense Factory and Codex, we are making agentic remediation practical, safe, and context-driven. From major vulnerability coordination like Patch the Planet to everyday code fixes in developer repos, this partnership helps organizations move from alert fatigue to rapid, reviewed remediation—defending at machine speed while keeping human judgment firmly at the center.Learn more: Open AI Daybreak Defense Factory, Wiz plugin for Codex

articles.title: Agentic Attacks: In The Wild
articles.context: Wiz Defend includes detections for these patterns and attackers, some of which are outlined both this post and the advisory
articles.full_text:
Wiz Research has been closely monitoring the evolving role of Agentic Offensive Frameworks in the threat landscape. We first covered this trend in our disclosure of attempts by Storm-0940, a Chinese-state aligned actor, to use ARTEX to conduct supply chain compromises into other software sectors. The next week, we shared the recurring fingerprints of agentic activity based on public and private cases. Then we closed out last month by sounding the alarm on Black October for AI Developer Platforms - linking nine disclosed incidents in an agentic attack trend.

We’ve also worked with our internal partners at Google Threat Intelligence Group in their coverage of Agentic Offensive Frameworks and the Significant Threshold that Agentic Threat Activity has crossed.

There has been explosive growth in successful agentic attacks, just in the last three weeks. Since publishing the Black October post, an additional twenty related incidents have been disclosed by vendors. Wiz’s CIRT has seen a 3x increase in engagement requests, matching the trend across the industry of overwhelming IR demand.

Wiz customers should review the Threat Center Advisory on this topic: AI Agent Frameworks Driving Cloud Intrusions: ARTEX and Related Tooling Indicators. Wiz Defend includes detections for these patterns and attackers, some of which are outlined both this post and the advisory.

Agentic Offensive Frameworks

The activity we’ve observed since late September 2026 uses ARTEX, its public forks and rebrands, and other agentic tools with a similar design.

ARTEX is only one of these frameworks: others seen in the wild include Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike, alongside offensive use of generic harness like Hermes, as well as custom offensive harnesses. ARTEX is open source and has hundreds of forks. Activity attributed to “ARTEX” comes from multiple unrelated operators and should not be read as a single campaign or attributed to one threat actor.

Cases

Wiz Research and CIRT have been hunting, tracking, observing, and responding to a broad set of agentic offensive frameworks attacks, some successful. In addition to the examples we’ve previously shared, we wanted to provide some cases emblematic of what we’re seeing in this new threat environment.

Opportunistic Campaigns Using Agentic Offensive Frameworks

The first pattern we see is broad, seemingly opportunistic attacks by actors who have gone all-in on agentic offensive frameworks. These campaigns are frequently:

Proxied through residential and ISP pools: Requests rotate through commercial residential proxy inventory, often a new exit for every single request. IP-based blocking and IOC sharing do very little.

Noisy: These agents spray passwords, create canary accounts, hammer sign-up and password-reset flows, and probe every available endpoint. They also label their own work: pentest, probe, recon, and incrementing task numbers show up in user agents, resource names and usernames.

Vector agnostic: The same operator will try stolen cloud keys, identity-provider OAuth flows, public sign-up flows, anonymous storage access and CI/CD trust, in parallel and across many organizations.

Once a foothold is found, it is used to explore lateral movement, harvest credentials and exfiltrate data.

We wanted to highlight a campaign, one of a dozen campaigns we’re tracking, which we have named "ARTEX-Harvester." We’ve clustered this campaign based on, among other signals, a distinctive boto3 build, incrementing Intent ID correlation cross-victim, and proxy pool usage overlap.

Between late October and mid-November 2026 we tied it, at varying confidence, to activity at more than a dozen organizations. It demonstrates exactly the patterns we highlighted. Almost every request used a different residential or ISP proxy exit - across more than 220 IPs in a single target.

Across the campaign, the same operator attempted:

Abuse of stolen credentials

Anonymous storage probing

Abuse of public sign-up, password-reset and sign-in flows

Identity-provider probing

Among the numerous attempted footholds, one success shows how these attacks progress once initial access is achieved.

Compromised VCS credentials allowed access to private repositories

The attack pivoted from CI to the cloud environment by creating branches that abused CI workload identity trust relationships.

Harvest workflows dumped CI-accessible secrets and Terraform state

Those secrets and repositories were exfiltrated

In parallel, the operator used a stolen service-account token from an application pod. That account could create privileged pods with the node's root filesystem mounted. The operator used that to deploy a "node-level collector" pod, which harvested the kubelet PKI and every projected service-account token on the node. One of those tokens, belonging to cert-manager, could read the ArgoCD secrets, leading to cluster-admin.

Detection

These attacks are far from stealthy. Wiz Issues captured this activity across a variety of rules that are agnostic to the usage of an Agentic Offensive Framework (see below).

Additionally, artifacts were heavily marked with agentic offensive framework self-labeling behavior, including pentest-recon user agents, pentest-* workspaces and pods, and an incrementing task intent counter (pentest-iNNNNNN).

Wiz Sensor caught the behavior within the cluster, including privileged container creation, nsenter, IMDS kube-env queries and drifted scripts reaching for cloud credentials.

Targeted Attacks and Open Directories

One of the more interesting byproducts of agentic offensive frameworks is a trend of poor operational security. ARTEX shipped with its web console exposed to the internet by default, often still on default credentials, and many operators never lock it down: Censys counted more than 1,400 exposed ARTEX consoles in early November.

The result is a steady supply of exposed command-and-control panels and open directories for threat intelligence and security firms to analyze.

Because these frameworks are agentic, those exposures reveal more than attacker actions. They capture the attack as a narrative: operator prompts, planner intents, agent transcripts and the model's own reasoning.

Seeing Both Sides of an Attack

This exposure occasionally grants something rare: both sides of the same intrusion. In some cases, we can pair our telemetry with the relevant attacker’s leaked logs and tools - granting a picture of not just what they did in a single incident, but what they did everywhere else, why they did it, and what they planned next.

Here is one such anonymized case:

Across four days in October, an attacker navigated two AWS accounts and seven EKS clusters:

Initial foothold: a stolen Terraform-runner session read the kubelet kubeconfig, then created a privileged pod and a cluster-admin binding.

CI compromise: remote code execution on the Jenkins controller opened a reverse shell to the attacker's server.

Node persistence: a pod escape put a custom loader on the nodes. It was an ld.so.preload userland rootkit with a DNS-tunnel channel, disguised as a fontconfig service, and had zero detections on VirusTotal.

Credential use off-platform: node, IRSA and Terraform-runner credentials were used from the attacker's own server to read Terraform state and Secrets Manager, and to open SSM sessions.

The attacker’s open directory colors in the details, across over 3,000 exposed files.

It shows activity outside the observed telemetry:

Identity provider: forged admin tokens gave access to 3,392 users and their live session tokens.

Bastion: beacons were pushed to 19 hosts, and the bastion's database was decrypted for 50 SSH private keys.

CI/CD: GitHub Actions secrets were dumped, and the production Jenkinsfile was modified to run before its approval gate, exposing production secrets.

It also shows more about the attacker’s operations:

Command layer: CyberStrikeAI ran the operation. A csai- prefix is on nearly everything the attacker created (csai-escape pods, a csai-pentest-role IAM role, a csai-probe runner).

Operator workspace: an ARTEX checkout sat alongside .claude, .grok and .agents directories. The same server ran ARTEX tooling against several other organizations that month, unsuccessfully.

Reporting: the operator's own auto-generated Chinese language report masks the intrusion as an "authorised red-team pentest" and claims 58 findings.

AI tools as targets: Anthropic API keys were harvested from 50 hosts, and employees' AI coding-assistant session histories were mined for production SSO credentials.

Black October Q4

Finally, let’s revisit “Black October for AI Developer Platforms.”

Since publishing the blog post, disclosed incidents have more than tripled. While insufficient details have been shared to link all these incidents to any single actor, or even agentic offensive frameworks in some cases, there is a clear trend where attackers are using agentic offensive frameworks to target rich sources of LLM access and credentials.

Where victims have disclosed a root cause, the entry points are familiar.

Stolen or leaked credentials (Zeabur, Kernel, Lightning AI, Bitrise)

Exposed or vulnerable services (Chainstack's default-credential Grafana, NEAR AI's SGLang RCE, Northflank's API zero-day)

Tenant-isolation escapes (Railway, Phala, Dokploy).

Increasingly, the way in was an upstream breach: keys and secrets stolen from one platform opened the next.

The impact is just as consistent. Attackers go straight for environment variables and stored customer secrets, prioritizing AI provider and cloud keys that can be validated, resold or burned on LLM usage within hours.

Recommendations

Wiz’s AI Threat Readiness Framework is our blueprint for how to build a security program that can stay ahead of these attacks. Defenders must put AI to work in order to leverage their context advantage against attackers and enable real machine-speed defense against these new tools and tactics.

Unusual Enumeration Activity by IAM User

articles.full_text:
On November 19, 2026, the PHP group published security updates addressing 17 vulnerabilities across all actively supported branches (PHP 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5). Seven of these flaws are rated Critical (CVSS 9.2) and present direct pathways to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Security teams are advised to identify and patch exposed PHP deployments, as earlier mitigation efforts implemented during October's response to "PHP2Shell" do not provide protection against all of these new exploit vectors. As of yet, no exploitation in the wild has been observed by Wiz or mentioned in public reporting.

What are these vulnerabilities?

phpAfterShell: File-Based Session Handling (CVE-2026-126714)

Reported by depthfirst, this vulnerability exists in PHP’s default file-based session handler (session.save_handler = files). When PHP writes session update progress (such as during unauthenticated file uploads), the file-write process is not atomic. If a PHP worker process is abruptly stopped during this write, due to memory limits or timeout settings, it can leave behind a partially written, malformed session file.

When a subsequent request calls session_start(), PHP attempts to deserialize this file. If the file's contents are carefully structured, this deserialization process can be manipulated to trigger an object deserialization primitive. This behavior bypasses the initial parameters set during October's PHP2Shell patches, making a fresh update necessary to secure file-based session pipelines.

PHP-FPM Request Smuggling (CVE-2026-129289)

This issue centers on how PHP-FPM processes unread request-body bytes before reusing a persistent connection. In environments where the front-end web server (such as Nginx or Apache) is configured to keep FastCGI connections open to the FPM backend, an unauthenticated user can structure a request to append a secondary, hidden FastCGI request within the request body.

Because the backend does not discard the leftover bytes, the subsequent request handled over that same connection executes the smuggled instructions. This allows a request to bypass front-end routing rules and execute with the privileges of the active FPM worker.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

The overall risk depends largely on your environment's configuration. PHP remains widely used, powering approximately 70% of websites with known server-side languages. While the technical severity of these bugs is high, executing them successfully requires specific conditions. For instance, phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) requires file-based sessions (the PHP default) and relies on finding an exploitable gadget chain in the application's code (which isn’t guaranteed to exist in every application) to achieve code execution.

Importantly, the vast majority of the other critical vulnerabilities in this release require non-default configurations or uncommon setups, such as enabling runtime-mixed session serializers, enabling PHP 8.5 exception arguments (zend.exception_ignore_args = 0), or writing startup warnings to a file-based error log on non-thread-safe builds. This ultimately means that default installations are naturally insulated from many of these vectors.

Which actions should security teams take?

A. Plan a Routine Upgrade

Plan to update your PHP installations to 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, or 8.2.36 (or 8.6.0).

Rebuild affected container images and restart the PHP-FPM master service or web server process to ensure the newly patched binaries are active in memory.

B. Temporary Configuration Adjustments (If patching is delayed)

Disable Session Upload Progress: If your application does not require tracking upload progress, disabling this feature in php.ini mitigates the primary attack path for phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) in particular: session.upload_progress.enabled = 0

Disable FastCGI Connection Reuse: Block the PHP-FPM request smuggling vector by configuring Nginx (fastcgi_keep_conn off) or Apache (enablereuse=off) to close backend connections immediately.

Configure Exception Arguments (PHP 8.5): Ensure exception arguments are omitted to mitigate CVE-2026-129474: zend.exception_ignore_args = 1

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.

NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server, it powers more than 225 million websites.

Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.

We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.

We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.

Responsible disclosure timeline

October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.

November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.

November 16, 2026: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.

November 17, 2026: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.

November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.

Overview

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.

Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.

What is NGINX?

NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server, powering more than 225 million websites. It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.

NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.

The Vulnerabilities

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Tracking ID

The bug

What an attacker can achieve

CVE-2026-123633

HTTP/2 connection use-after-free

Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow

Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.

Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.

Impact

On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.

An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.

Coordinated disclosure

We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.

Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.

Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities.

Technical deep dive

CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable

NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.

We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:

ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1);

if (h2c->state.incomplete) {

return;

}

When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing. However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.

Triggering the use-after-free

Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.

Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection(). When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.

Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.

From use-after-free to remote code execution

The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection.

This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow

Returning credit for unsent data

HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window.

When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:

h2c->send_window += window;

This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.

A bounds check that no longer works

The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update(), which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window)

The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.

From an invalid length to remote code execution

The invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.

When the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.

Exploitation

To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.

Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.

Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation.

Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.

How Can Wiz Help?

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Conclusion

With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.

As we saw with PHP2Shell, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.

The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.

Stay in touch

Hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

articles.title: CVE-2026-114938 OpenJDK RCE (Java4Shell): Everything You Need to Know
articles.context: The "Java4Shell" vulnerability and exploit were discovered and disclosed by security firm Calif
articles.full_text:
On November 17, 2026, details emerged exposing a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in OpenJDK, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (dubbed "Java4Shell") with a CVSSv4.0 score of 9.2. The bug exists in the optimized assembly code handling AVX-512 Base64 decoding, allowing remote unauthenticated attackers to cause heap memory corruption. Triggering this flaw on affected systems can lead to remote code execution.

The "Java4Shell" vulnerability and exploit were discovered and disclosed by security firm Calif.

What is CVE-2026-114938?

CVE-2026-114938 is a memory-corruption vulnerability residing in the optimized Base64 decoding intrinsic engine of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). To maximize performance, OpenJDK uses an optimized implementation on supported x86-64 processors, based on AVX-512 VBMI instructions. However, the optimized assembly code miscalculates the output array bounds when handling inputs that contain an unexpected number of trailing padding characters (=).

When an input containing a specific sequence -such as 64 A characters followed by a single = - is parsed, the decoder's length calculation underflows to a negative value. This calculation mismatch causes an out-of-bounds write past the allocated heap memory buffer. Attackers can leverage this to overwrite adjacent object metadata, which can lead to code execution. We have proved that remote exploitation is feasible against standard Java applications such Jenkins, Confluence, and Apache Tomcat.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

Like other memory safety issues, exploitation is possible with AI, but is not trivial. Our AI based vulnerability research harness, Wiz Atlas, managed to find and build a proof-of-concept exploit for this vulnerability within 2 hours, even before the full details were disclosed. Having said that, generalizing the exploit for an arbitrary target is difficult. We should expect adversaries to target commonplace Java applications, where specific builds and memory layouts repeat across targets. Motivated adversaries may tailor exploits with AI for specific targets, including home-grown applications.

Web Application Firewalls can help mitigate some of the exploits as they emerge in the wild. Since this vulnerability is rooted in OpenJDK itself, many possible code paths using user inputs may lead into the vulnerable code path, so it’s unlikely that WAF rules will be able to cover all possible paths, and will never be able to cover home grown applications completely. The best solution is upgrading to the latest OpenJDK version.

Prioritize externally facing, packaged Java applications, and make sure they are either patched or restricted from public access. Upgrade home-grown Java applications and update to the latest OpenJDK version containing the fix.

Which products are affected?

The vulnerability affects OpenJDK versions 17.0.6 and later, as well as downstream distributions, provided they run on x86-64 hardware supporting AVX-512 VBMI instruction sets (ARM64 processors are unaffected). Affected software distributions and hardware include:

OpenJDK Distributions: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, and Oracle Java SE (specifically versions 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3).

Vulnerable CPU Architectures: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids) and AMD EPYC/Ryzen (Zen 4 or newer).

Proven Vulnerable Applications (Pre-Auth RCE): Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and custom frameworks built on Spring Boot, Apache Struts, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Netflix Spinnaker and Apache Tomcat.

Which actions should security teams take?

Security teams should immediately prioritize the following mitigation steps:

Audit and Patch: Identify all systems running OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later on AVX-512-capable x86-64 hardware. Apply the official security patches released on November 17, 2026, or update to downstream vendor-supplied builds immediately.

Verify Hardware Vulnerability: Run the following command on Linux systems to check if your infrastructure is physically affected:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

If all four CPU flags are present in the output, the host runs the vulnerable hardware execution path.

Implement JVM Runtime Workarounds: If immediate patching is not possible, apply one of the following flags to JVM startup parameters to completely neutralize the vulnerability. They may have performance impact on the application.

Disable Base64 Intrinsics (Recommended): -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

Disable AVX-512 execution (x86-64 only): -XX:UseAVX=2

Isolate Internet-Facing Services: Temporarily restrict external network access to vulnerable management portals (e.g., Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak) until mitigations or updates are deployed.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

articles.title: Microsoft agent-framework Compromised: Credential Stealer Targets Azure and CI Pipelines
articles.context: As of 21:30 UTC, both versions were no longer available on PyPI
articles.full_text:
At 20:35 UTC on November 17, 2026, a malicious version (1.26.1) of the agent-framework package (Microsoft Agent Framework) was uploaded to PyPI. A second version, 1.26.2, followed at 21:08 UTC. As of 21:30 UTC, both versions were no longer available on PyPI. The package gets about 41,000 downloads a week.

The most recent safe version is 1.26.0.

When a malicious version is installed, it drops a .pth file into the site-packages root (agent_framework_meta.pth in 1.26.1, af_runtime_diag.pth in 1.26.2). Python runs .pth files on every interpreter start, so the credential stealer runs whenever Python starts in that environment, even if agent-framework is never imported.

Root Cause

The root cause hasn't been confirmed. What we know so far:

There is no python-1.26.1 tag or release in microsoft/agent-framework, and the main branch doesn't contain the malicious code.

Legitimate releases publish a wheel and an sdist together with agent-framework-core of the same version. 1.26.1 was a wheel only, and still depends on agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0.

This indicates 1.26.1 may have been built outside the project's normal release process and uploaded directly to PyPI.

Earlier this year, another Microsoft Python package, durabletask, was compromised after its PyPI token was stolen. We have not linked the two incidents.

Payload

agent_framework_meta.pth contains one line: import agent_framework_meta

In 1.26.1, agent_framework_meta/__init__.py then calls _telemetry._start(). The stealer forks into a detached session (os.setsid()), or falls back to a daemon thread where fork isn't available. It sets _AF_TEL=1 to avoid running again in child processes.

The file and function names (_telemetry, "Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook", user-agent af-runtime-diagnostics/1) are made to look like legitimate SDK telemetry.

Credential Stealer

The stealer is focused on Azure and Azure DevOps. It collects:

Environment variables with names containing strings such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, FOUNDRY, NPM, PIP, NUGET, SYSTEM, BUILD, AGENT

Other processes' environments: secret-looking values read from up to 300 /proc/*/environ files

Credential files (up to 60):

Azure CLI (~/.azure/)

.npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json

Hugging Face tokens

Azure DevOps agent .credentials

.env and JSON files under /app and /workspace

Azure DevOps OIDC tokens: if SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are set, it requests an OIDC token for api://AzureADTokenExchange

Azure managed-identity tokens from IMDS or the App Service identity endpoint for 12 resources: ARM, Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, Azure AI/ML, Search, Container Registry, Azure DevOps, and AzureADTokenExchange

Azure instance metadata

Everything is put into one JSON document, zlib-compressed, base64-encoded, and sent in one HTTPS POST to webhook[.]site. The URL is hardcoded and the payload has no fallback channel. Failures are silently ignored and not retried.

Version 1.26.2

1.26.2 was uploaded at 21:08 UTC, 33 minutes after 1.26.1. It is a repacked 1.26.1 that sends to the same webhook.site URL, with these changes:

New trigger. agent_framework_meta/__init__.py is restored to the clean 1.26.0 file. Instead, a new top-level af_runtime_diag.pth imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, which starts the stealer as soon as it is imported. Searching only for the 1.26.1 file names will miss this version.

GitHub Actions OIDC theft. In workflows with id-token: write, it requests OIDC tokens for api://AzureADTokenExchange and https://management.azure.com/. Where an Entra ID federated credential trusts the workflow, these tokens can be exchanged for Azure access, with no stored secret needed.

Wider collection. Environment-variable matching now includes ACTIONS, OIDC, RUNNER and ARM_. GitHub-hosted runner paths (/home/runner/work/_temp/*, /home/runner/.azure/) were added, and the file cap rose from 60 to 80.

New User-Agent: runtime-diagnostics/1

How webhook.site limits the impact

webhook.site is a public request-inspection service. On its free tier, a URL that isn't attached to an account:

accepts at most 100 requests. After that, new requests get HTTP 410 Gone or 429 Too Many Requests and are not logged.

expires after 7 days.

We have confirmed the attackers token was on the free tier, and a maximum of 50 requests were captured. However, those requests can contain working cloud, CI and registry credentials.

Identify exposure: search lockfiles, CI logs, virtualenvs and container images for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. Pin to 1.26.0.
